items.answer: I'll use a sliding window with a hash set. Initialize left=0, right=0, max_len=0. Advance right; if s[right] is already in the set, advance left until we remove it. Update max_len = max(max_len, right - left + 1). Time: O(n), Space: O(k) where k is the character set size. Edge cases: empty string returns 0; all-same chars returns 1; all-unique returns full length.
items.label_notes: Correct approach, O(n) explicitly stated, edge cases mentioned, clear communication.

items.answer: Use a sliding window. I'll have two pointers and move the right pointer forward. When I see a duplicate I move the left pointer. Track the maximum length seen. Should be O(n) time.
items.label_notes: Correct approach and complexity stated, but no edge cases and communication is thin.

items.answer: I would check every substring using two for loops and use a set to check for repeating characters. For each starting position try all end positions. If the substring has no duplicates, update the max. This is O(n^2) time.
items.label_notes: Brute force O(n^2) — correct but not optimal. Partial credit on correctness, low on complexity.

items.answer: I'll use ReentrantLock with two Condition objects: notFull and notEmpty. put() acquires the lock, loops while size==capacity awaiting notFull, adds the item, then signals notEmpty. take() loops while empty awaiting notEmpty, removes, signals notFull. Using while-loops (not if) guards against spurious wakeups. Testing: I'd use CountDownLatch to coordinate producer/consumer threads and verify ordering. Lock is released in finally blocks.
items.label_notes: Correct blocking semantics, spurious wakeup handled, testing mentioned, while vs if explained.

items.answer: Use synchronized methods. Make put() and get() synchronized. If the queue is full in put(), throw an exception. If empty in get(), return null. Use an ArrayList internally.
items.label_notes: Not blocking — throws/returns instead of blocking. Missing the core concurrent semantics requirement.

items.answer: API gateway accepts payment with idempotency key (stored in Redis with TTL). Kafka topic for async processing — producers write payment events, consumers commit offsets after processing. Outbox pattern in the payment service: write to DB and outbox table in one transaction, a separate relay reads the outbox and publishes to Kafka (at-least-once). PostgreSQL event-sourced audit log — every state change is an append-only row. Shard by merchant_id for horizontal scale. Balance check via read replica + optimistic locking on account table.
items.label_notes: Idempotency, Kafka, outbox pattern, event sourcing, sharding all covered. Solid system design.

items.answer: I'd use a microservices architecture. A payment service receives requests and publishes to a message queue. A processor service consumes and updates the database. For idempotency, store a request ID. Use a relational database for the audit log. Scale by adding more processor instances.
items.label_notes: Correct direction but superficial. Idempotency mentioned but no dedup mechanism. Kafka implied but not named. No outbox or event sourcing.

items.answer: Situation: my team chose MongoDB for a payments ledger without a full review. Task: I was concerned about ACID guarantees for financial data. Action: I wrote a design doc comparing Mongo vs Postgres on durability, transaction semantics, and rollback. I presented it with a concrete example of a multi-account transfer that would be inconsistent in Mongo without transactions. I proposed a 2-week spike to prototype the Postgres path. Result: the team agreed, we switched, and in 18 months we had zero consistency incidents. I learned to raise architectural concerns early with evidence rather than opinion.
items.label_notes: Full STAR, specific and technical, measurable outcome, learning articulated.
